title: Conditional Probability
presenterNotes: Block 1: Emphasize the table method for conditional probabilities. The formula P(B|A) = (number in A and B)/(number in A) is intuitive when using a two‑way table.
Block 2: Independence vs. dependence is a crucial distinction. Use the coin/die vs. cards without replacement examples. The formal definition via conditional probability is important.
Block 3: The Multiplication Rule ties conditional probability and independence together. Work through both dependent and independent examples, stressing when to use which.
Block 4: The 'at least one' shortcut with the complement is a powerful technique. Drill it with several examples; it appears frequently in later chapters.
Block 5: The blueprint summarizes all problem types. Encourage students to first identify what they're asked to find, then pick the right formula. The decision flowchart is a good reference.

examples.prompt: Two cards are drawn from a standard deck without replacement. Find the probability the second card is a queen, given the first is a king.
examples.title: Example A – Cards Without Replacement
steps: Given the first card was a king, the deck now has 51 cards, with all 4 queens still present.
So the conditional probability is: $ P(\text{Queen second} \mid \text{King first}) = \frac{4}{51} \approx 0.078 $.
Note that without the condition, $ P(\text{Queen}) = 4/52 \approx 0.077 $. They differ because the events are dependent.

explanation: A [[kw:conditional probability]] is the probability of an event occurring, given that another event has already occurred.
The notation $ P(B \mid A) $ reads 'the probability of $ B $, given $ A $'.
To compute $ P(B \mid A) $, restrict the sample space to only those outcomes in event $ A $, then find the fraction of those that are in $ B $.

Formula: $ P(B \mid A) = \frac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(A)} $, or when outcomes are equally likely, $ P(B \mid A) = \frac{\text{Number of outcomes in both } A \text{ and } B}{\text{Number of outcomes in } A} $.

confusionCorner.title: $P(B \mid A)$ Is Not $P(A \mid B)$
confusionCorner.body: These two conditional probabilities are usually different. For example, $ P(\text{High IQ} \mid \text{Gene}) $ is not the same as $ P(\text{Gene} \mid \text{High IQ}) $. [[imp:Read the 'given' part carefully — it defines the reduced sample space.]]

formulaCard.title: Independence Test
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{If } P(B \mid A) = P(B) \;\Longrightarrow\; A \text{ and } B \text{ are independent}$$ $$\text{If } P(B \mid A) \neq P(B) \;\Longrightarrow\; A \text{ and } B \text{ are dependent}$$

rows.2: Yes. Each surgery's outcome is independent of others.

explanation: Two events $A$ and $B$ are [[kw:independent]] if the occurrence of one does [[imp:not affect]] the probability of the other.
Formally, $A$ and $B$ are independent if $ P(B \mid A) = P(B) $ or equivalently $ P(A \mid B) = P(A) $.
If $ P(B \mid A) \neq P(B) $, the events are [[kw:dependent]].
Examples: Coin toss and die roll are independent. Drawing cards without replacement is dependent.
Real-world examples: Smoking and lung disease are dependent; eye color and favorite food are likely independent.

confusionCorner.title: Independence ≠ Mutual Exclusivity
confusionCorner.body: Do not confuse independent with mutually exclusive. Independent events can occur together; mutually exclusive events cannot. In fact, mutually exclusive events with non‑zero probabilities are always [[imp:dependent]] because if one occurs, the other cannot.

blocks.title: Independent and Dependent Events

discoveryHook.scenario: Some events have no influence on each other — like tossing a coin and rolling a die. Others do — like drawing two cards without replacement. Identifying independence is crucial because it simplifies probability calculations dramatically.

examples.title: Example A – Identifying Independence
examples.prompt: Decide if the events are independent: (1) Selecting a king, not replacing it, then selecting a queen. (2) Tossing a head, then rolling a 6.
steps: For cards without replacement: $ P(\text{Queen}) = 4/52 $, but $ P(\text{Queen} \mid \text{King}) = 4/51 $. They are not equal → [[kw:dependent]].
For coin and die: $ P(6) = 1/6 $, $ P(6 \mid H) = 1/6 $. Equal → [[kw:independent]].
The key is whether the first event changes the probability of the second.

Explain to a partner: Why does 'increased risk' imply dependence?
steps: If they were independent, having sleep apnea would not change the probability of high blood pressure.
'Increased risk' means $ P(\text{High BP} \mid \text{Apnea}) > P(\text{High BP}) $.
Because the probability changes, the events are [[kw:dependent]].
Many medical conditions are dependent events.

The gene appears to lower the chance of high IQ slightly in this sample.

discoveryHook.scenario: Want to know the chance of a king followed by a queen? Or of three successful surgeries in a row? The Multiplication Rule combines individual event probabilities — adjusting for dependence when needed — to give you the probability of a sequence of events.

explanation: The [[kw:Multiplication Rule]] finds the probability that two events $A$ and $B$ occur in sequence.
General formula: $ P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A) $.
If $A$ and $B$ are [[imp:independent]], then $ P(B \mid A) = P(B) $, so the rule simplifies to: $ P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \cdot P(B) $.
The rule can be extended to more than two events: for independent events, multiply their probabilities; for dependent events, adjust each conditional probability accordingly.

rows.1: $ P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A) $

formulaCard.title: Multiplication Rule Formulas
formulaCard.formula: $$P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A)$$ $$\text{If independent: } P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$$

confusionCorner.title: Don't Multiply Unconditionally!
confusionCorner.body: If events are dependent, you must use $ P(B \mid A) $, not $ P(B) $. Forgetting to check independence can lead to wrong probabilities. [[imp:Always ask: Does the first event change the probability of the second?]]

explanation: The phrase '[[imp:at least one]]' means one or more occurrences.
The complement of 'at least one' is '[[imp:none]]' (zero occurrences).
Thus, $ P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none}) $.
This method is especially useful when the events are independent, because $ P(\text{none}) $ can be computed by multiplying the probabilities of each individual failure.

formulaCard.formula: $$P(\text{at least one success}) = 1 - P(\text{all failures})$$ $$\text{For independent events: } P(\text{all failures}) = (P(\text{failure}))^n$$
formulaCard.title: The 'At Least One' Shortcut

examples.title: Example A – At Least One Surgery Succeeds
examples.prompt: Knee surgery has a success probability of 0.85. Three surgeries are performed. Find the probability that at least one is successful.
steps: Success probability = 0.85, so failure probability = $ 1 - 0.85 = 0.15 $.
The complement of 'at least one success' is 'all fail'.
$ P(\text{at least one success}) = 1 - 0.003375 = 0.996625 \approx 0.997 $.
It's almost certain that at least one surgery succeeds.

examples.peerPrompt:

Explain to a partner: How does the complement method reduce work when $n$ is large?
steps: With 3 surgeries, there are 7 success‑containing patterns; with 10 surgeries, there would be $2^{10} - 1 = 1023$ patterns.
The complement method replaces many calculations with one: $ 1 - P(\text{all fail}) $.
This scales easily: $ P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - (P(\text{failure}))^n $.
It's a powerful shortcut for independent repeated trials.
examples.prompt: For three surgeries, the outcomes with at least one success are SSS, SSF, SFS, FSS, SFF, FSF, FFS — 7 patterns. Explain why the complement method is preferable.

Example C – Blood Type
examples.prompt: The probability a person in the U.S. has type B+ blood is 9%. Five people are selected at random. Find the probability at least one has B+ blood.
steps: $ P(\text{none B+}) = 0.91^5 \approx 0.624 $.
$ P(\text{at least one B+}) = 1 - 0.624 = 0.376 $.
There's about a 37.6% chance that at least one of the five has B+ blood.

discoveryHook.scenario: Three surgeries, each with an 85% success rate. You want the probability that at least one succeeds. Listing all 7 success-failure patterns is tedious. The complement method — finding the chance that all fail and subtracting from 1 — is a brilliant shortcut.

explanation: Blueprint steps: [[imp:Understand → Solve → Conclude]].

1. [[kw:Understand]]: Read the problem. Define events $A$ and $B$. Determine if they are independent or dependent. Identify if you need $P(A \text{ and } B)$, $P(B \mid A)$, or $P(\text{at least one})$.

2. [[kw:Solve]]: Select the appropriate rule. For conditional probability: $ P(B \mid A) = \frac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(A)} $. For sequence: $ P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A) $ (or $P(A) \cdot P(B)$ if independent). For 'at least one': $ 1 - P(\text{none}) $.
3. [[kw:Conclude]]: Compute the probability and interpret in context. Round appropriately. Check if the event is unusual ($P \leq 0.05$).

formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Problem} \;\begin{cases} \text{Given } A, \text{ find } B & \;\rightarrow\; P(B \mid A) \\ \text{Sequence of events} & \;\begin{cases} \text{Independent} & \;\rightarrow\; P(A) \cdot P(B) \\ \text{Dependent} & \;\rightarrow\; P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A) \end{cases} \\ \text{At least one} & \;\rightarrow\; 1 - P(\text{none}) \end{cases}$$

legend.meaning: Identify independence first; it determines which multiplication rule to use.

confusionCorner.body: In conditional probability from tables, the denominator is the total of the given condition's row or column, not the grand total. A common mistake is using the overall total instead. [[imp:Always circle the 'given' group and use its size.]]
